newsitem.title: UK: UK Tory "Demon Eyes" ads well-remembered -survey.
newsitem.headline: UK Tory "Demon Eyes" ads well-remembered -survey.

text.p: The "Demon Eyes" poster advertisements run by Britain's Tory party have been well remembered by viewers, but the "Same Old Tories, Same Old Lies" poster ads run by the opposition Labour party are better liked, according to a survey released on Wednesday.

"The battle of political poster advertisements between the Tories and Labour is just about even according to the first results of independent research into the parties' recent political campaigns," Maiden Outdoor, the outdoor advertising contractor which commissioned and analysed the survey, said in a statement.
The survey, conducted by RSL Signpost, compared responses to the Tory ads "New Labour, New Danger" and "Labour's Union Jack" to Labour's "Same Old Tories, Same Old Lies" poster ad.
Dubbed the "Demon Eyes" ad, the "New Labour, New Danger" poster showed Labour leader Tony Blair with demonic red eyes and a manic grin peering through net curtains.

The ad, designed by Maurice and Charles Saatchi, sparked a storm of critcism when it debuted in August, drawing fire from church leaders, newspaper writers and even some Conservative members of Parliament.
Maiden said 72 percent of respondents remembered seeing the Tory campaign and 57 percent correctly attributed it to the Tories. But 64 percent of the respondents said they did not like the ad.
By contrast, 47 percent of respondents remembered seeing the Labour campaign and 41 percent attributed it correctly. But 48 percent of the respondents liked the ad.
The Tory posters were more successful with men than with women and were more successful with upper income individuals known as ABC1s and with 18- to 24-year-olds.

The Labour campaign was better remembered and more correctly attributed by men, but men and women liked it in equal proportions, Maiden reported. The Labour campaign appealed most to 35- to 44-year-olds and to ABs.
"In the context of brand advertising, these are very good scores," Francis Goodwin, managing director of Maiden Roadside, said in a statement.

Poster advertising is expected to be a crucial battleground for Britains' political parties in the runup to the next campaign, which must be held by May 1997. "Because of the medium's power and impact, million of pounds will be spent on political advertising on the streets," Maiden said.

RSL Signpost conducts monthly consumer surveys on poster ads, interviewing 300 individuals at 10 locations in the Greater London area. Respondents are show photographs of ads with the brand name of the product or service removed and asked if they have seen the campaign, whether they remember the brand, whether they liked the campaign, and whether they are more likely to buy the product.
